paper_title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment. Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and evolving only one component is suboptimal---a harness tuned for one checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed harness. In light of this, we propose Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness proposer. Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step). The policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the policy's evolving failure modes. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings. Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. Self-HPO also improves reliability (Pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (Pass@k) over the base agent. Additionally, we show that with a stronger external model (e.g., Opus 4.8) as the harness proposer, the same framework yields a further performance boost.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents have made rapid progress on complex, multi-step tasks such as software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024), web navigation (Zhou et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025c), and computer use (Xie et al., 2024; Agashe et al., 2025). Such an agent consists of two components: the policy model and its harness, which is the external scaffold that decides what the model observes, how its actions are executed, what feedback it receives, and when an episode terminates (Yao et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Typically, the policy model defines the agents capability boundary, while the harness determines how these capabilities are elicited, hence the same model may succeed or fail on one problem depending on its harness (Le et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). There have been two main lines of research on improving such agents. Harness optimization holds the policy fixed and searches over prompts, workflows, or agent code (Hu et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), whereas policy optimization holds the harness fixed and updates the model from successful trajectories or verifiable rewards (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025a). However, harness-only optimization cannot improve the underlying model, while policy-only training can learn only from the trajectories that its fixed harness elicits. In this work, we introduce Self-HPO, framework for recursive self-improvement driven by the agents own policy. As illustrated in Figure 1, Self-HPO alternates harness optimization (H-step) with policy optimization under the optimized harness (P-step). Harness optimization exposes and compensates for the weaknesses of the current policy, while policy optimization internalizes the elicited behaviors into the model and shifts the failures that the next harness should target. Specifically, in the H-step, the current policy analyzes its failed trajectories and proposes harness revisions targeting its own failure modes, and selects the updated harness based on search-set performance (2.2). In the P-step, the policy is updated using reinforcement learning under the optimized harness (2.3). In the next H-step, the updated policy serves as the harness proposer, with hard tasks identified from the preceding P-step as the search set to keep harness search aligned with the policys evolving failure modes. We instantiate Self-HPO with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the base policy, and miniSWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) as the seed harness. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only optimization, with the average resolve rate improving at every optimization step, as demonstrated in Figure 1. On SWE-Bench Verified (Chowdhury et al., 2024), it improves the base resolve rate from 61.0% to 69.5%, with transferable gains on the out-of-distribution SWE-Bench Multilingual (Yang et al., 2025) and SWE-Bench Pro (Deng et al., 2025). Ablations further show that evolving the harness search set with hard tasks identified during policy learning yields better performance than reusing fixed set. We also extend Self-HPO to the external-model setup where Opus 4.8 is used as an external harness proposer, which further raises the resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified to 71.6%. The main contributions of this work are as follows: We propose Self-HPO, recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, where the agent uses its own policy as the harness proposer and adapts harness search to the policys evolving failure modes. We demonstrate that Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only baselines across three coding benchmarks, improving the average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings. Our study shows that both optimized components of Self-HPO retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. We also find that Self-HPO not only improves reliability (pass@1) but also expands the capability frontier (pass@k) of the agent.

The harness changes which behaviors the current policy can reliably express, while policy update changes the failures that the next harness should target. As shown in Figure 2, each H-step holds the policy fixed while using it to analyze failures and propose harness revisions, and each P-step then freezes this harness and updates the policy through reinforcement learning. The updated policy becomes the next harness proposer, with hard tasks identified from the training process forming the next search set. We call this alternating framework Harness-Policy Optimization (HPO) and implement it in two setups. In the self-improving setup (Self-HPO), the evolving policy proposes its own harness candidates, so no separate proposer model is needed. The H-step uses the frozen Pt as both task solver and harness proposer. The current pair (Ht, Pt) first generates trajectories on St, and the proposer inspects the current failures and produces targeted revisions to the prompt or executable runtime logic (see prompt in Appendix D). Each of the search iterations revises the current best harness, starting from Ht, using the accumulated experience of all evaluated harnesses and their trajectories. All candidates are evaluated on the same search set St. Evolving search set. The search set remains fixed within an H-step but evolves between rounds. For initialization, we sample S0 uniformly from D. Subsequent search sets consist of hard tasks identified from the training trajectories generated during the preceding P-step, where task is considered hard if it is never resolved in any of its rollouts in that P-step. The next H-step regenerates trajectories on those hard tasks with the updated harnesspolicy pair, producing fresh failure evidence for proposal. Harness search therefore follows the failures exposed by the preceding policy update instead of repeatedly optimizing against the initial tasks.

An executable verifier assigns binary outcome rewards, and our default optimizer combines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) with Balanced Adaptive Rollout (BAR) from Orchard (Peng et al., 2026). sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: 3.1 Experimental Setup Harness, model, and data. All experiments use Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the base policy and mini-SWE-agent (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024) as the seed harness. Following Orchard (Peng et al., 2026), we construct training set of 2,484 tasks from SWE-rebench (Badertdinov et al., 2025), SWE-rebench V2 (Badertdinov et al., 2026), and Scale-SWE (Zhao et al., 2026), which is used for both harness search and policy optimization. We perform two rounds of alternating harness and policy optimization based on the stopping criterion, with = 6 harness candidates per H-step and 50 RL updates per P-step. Appendix describes the implementation details. Benchmarks and evaluation metrics. SWE-Bench Verified (SWE-Verified) contains 500 humanvalidated GitHub issues and is our primary benchmark (Jimenez et al., 2024; Chowdhury et al., 2024). We further evaluate out-of-distribution performance on SWE-Bench Multilingual (SWE-Multi; 300 tasks) (Yang et al., 2025) and the public V2 set of SWE-Bench Pro (SWE-Pro; 642 tasks) (Deng et al., 2025), covering other programming languages and more diverse repository-level tasks. We report resolve rate, the percentage of tasks whose generated patches pass the benchmark verifier. Main results are averaged over three evaluation runs (avg@3) with standard deviations. Baselines. We compare our method with policy-only and harness-only baselines under two setups, with the base agent as reference. In the self-improving setup, RLVR (Peng et al., 2026) updates the policy under the seed harness, whereas Self-Harness (Zhang et al., 2026a) optimizes the harness using the base policy as proposer without updating its weights. Self-HPO alternates both updates and uses the current policy to propose harness changes. In the external-model setup, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from resolved Opus 4.8 trajectories on the same training tasks, while Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) uses Opus 4.8 to optimize the harness with the target policy fixed. HPO combines external harness proposals with RL policy updates.

As shown in Table 1, jointly optimizing the harness and policy achieves the best performance on all three benchmarks within each setup. Without an external proposer, Self-HPO reaches 69.5% on SWEVerified, outperforming RLVR and Self-Harness by 2.0 and 4.3 points, respectively. Its average score improves from 57.8% for Base to 64.8%, exceeding the stronger single-component baseline, RLVR, by 2.9 points. The same pattern holds with external supervision: HPO surpasses Meta-Harness by 2.5 points on SWE-Verified and 2.8 points on average. These consistent gains support optimizing the harness and policy together. Appendix further compares these results with frontier models on SWE-Verified. The gains generalize to out-of-distribution benchmarks. Although harness search and policy optimization use only tasks from Python projects, the gains transfer to SWE-Multi, which covers nine non-Python languages, and SWE-Pro, which spans broader range of languages and engineering tasks. Self-HPO achieves 59.7% and 65.2%, respectively, improving over Base by 5.5 and 6.9 points and over RLVR by 3.4 points on both benchmarks. The benefit is particularly clear on SWE-Multi, where Self-Harness improves over Base by only 0.1 point, compared with 5.5 points for Self-HPO. The same trend holds in the external-model setup, where HPO reaches 61.4% and 66.0%, outperforming both single-component baselines. These results show that the benefits of joint harnesspolicy optimization extend beyond the Python training domain. Learning from Opus 4.8 through harness optimization is more effective than SFT distillation. SFT and Meta-Harness represent two different approaches for transferring knowledge from Opus 4.8: SFT distills generated trajectories into the model weights, whereas Meta-Harness uses external proposals to optimize the harness while keeping the model fixed. Meta-Harness outperforms SFT by 4.1 points on SWE-Verified and 8.9 points on average. The gap is largest out of domain: SFT falls below Base on both SWE-Multi and SWE-Pro, while Meta-Harness improves on both. HPO further improves on Meta-Harness, indicating that policy optimization remains beneficial when coupled with an optimized harness. Alternating harness and policy optimization drives continued agent improvement. Figure 3 traces the optimization trajectories of Self-HPO and the two one-sided baselines. Self-HPO and Self-Harness begin with the same first H-step, but their trajectories diverge once Self-HPO updates its policy. Across all three benchmarks, the second H-step improves the updated Self-HPO policy, and the following P-step provides further gain. In contrast, another harness-only update does not consistently improve performance: Self-Harness drops from 55.0% to 54.3% on SWE-Multi. The final Self-HPO pair surpasses both single-component baselines on every benchmark, supporting repeated adaptation of the harness to the evolving policy. Figure 6 in the appendix provides candidate-level view of harness search on SWE-Verified.

To examine whether the gains persist beyond pass@1, Figures 4a and 4b compare Base and the final Self-HPO pair using eight attempts per task on SWE-Verified. As shown in Figure 4a, Self-HPO remains above Base for every from 1 to 8, and pass@8 increases from 80.0% to 84.8%, gain of 4.8 points. Figure 4b shows pass@1 gains of 17.2 and 12.9 points on Medium and Easy tasks, where Base sometimes succeeds but remains inconsistent, and 6.1-point gain on Hard tasks. At the same time, Self-HPOs pass@1 decreases by 2.2 points on the Resolved group, showing that improvement is not uniform across tasks. Together, the gains on Medium and Easy tasks demonstrate improved reliability, while the gains on Hard tasks and the higher pass@8 show the expanded capability frontier. Self-HPO reduces zero-success rollout groups during training. During the final Self-HPO P-step (Figure 4c), the fraction of zero-success groups, in which no rollout succeeds, declines to 6.5% over the final ten updates, whereas it remains mostly between 11% and 17% over the last 50 updates of RLVR. Under binary outcome rewards, such groups give GRPO no within-group reward contrast, so reducing them alleviates reward sparsity during policy optimization. 3.5 Case Studies Harness evolution adds targeted controls around the existing agent loop. Figure 5 contrasts the seed harness with the harness obtained after HPOs second H-step. The optimized harness retains the underlying model-query and command-execution loop, but intervenes before budget exhaustion and at submission. First, it warns the model as the step or time limit approaches and prompts best-effort submission before the episode ends with an empty result. Second, one-time empty-patch guard asks the model to include newly created files via git add -N. Third, it delays the first submission that passes the empty-patch guard to prompt check of API names and signatures against the repository and tests. Finally, fallback uses the sandboxs Git diff when the submitted patch fails the apply check. These changes target distinct ways in which useful repository edits can fail to become valid submission. They combine explicit runtime checks, such as detecting an empty patch, with behavioral guidance, such as requesting an interface check. Harness optimization can therefore change execution and termination logic, in addition to prompts. Appendix gives detailed diff against the seed harness together with the injected messages, and Appendix walks through task on which an evolved harness changes the outcome for the same policy.

Other work studies continual adaptation (Liu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b), task selection (Miyai et al., 2026), generalization through search controls and modular edits (Zhang et al., 2026d; Xia et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026), and fixed-budget evaluation (Ursekar et al., 2026). These methods adapt the agent around fixed task-solving policy, whereas Self-HPO also updates the policy that the harness serves. Policy learning and self-improvement. Iterative training uses filtered reasoning (Zelikman et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2023), refreshed preferences (Chen et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Pang et al., 2024), self-play curricula (Zhao et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026c;a), negative teachers (Pei et al., 2026), or evolving environments (Huang et al., 2026b). Software engineering agents learn from executable environments (Pan et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025), software-evolution supervision (Wei et al., 2025a), and self-play code repair (Wei et al., 2025b; Choi et al., 2026). Policy improvement also draws on verifiable-reward RL (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2026), harness-guided distillation (Ye et al., 2026b), and test-time learning during solution search (Wang et al., 2025b; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026). These methods train the policy under fixed harness, whereas in Self-HPO the harness co-evolves with the policy being trained. Joint harnesspolicy evolution. Joint adaptation spans prompts and weights (Soylu et al., 2024; Tiwari et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026e; Lu et al., 2026), executable harnesses and policies (Hebbar et al., 2026; Karten et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c; Kim et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b;a), and policies with evolving skills or external state (Xia et al., 2026a; Fu et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Ning et al., 2026), including safety-oriented co-evolution (Mao et al., 2026). MetaRSI composes data generation, harness editing, and model training within self-improvement loop (Tan et al., 2026). Concurrent work traces interventions (Fan & Huang, 2026), studies transfer and multiharness training (Le et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026a), and separates the ability to edit harness from the ability to benefit from one (Lin et al., 2026b). Self-HPO differs from these methods along two axes. First, the policy trained in the P-step becomes the harness proposer of the next H-step, whereas WHALE (Kim et al., 2026) keeps frozen external proposer and Evo2 (Xu et al., 2026a) trains separate proposer for frozen solver. HASE (Luo et al., 2026) also trains self-proposing policy, but places harness edits in the RL action space instead of alternating harness search with RL. Second,

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Self-HPO, recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization. The evolving policy proposes its own harness revisions, learns through RL under the selected harness, and supplies hard tasks for the next round of harness search. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only baselines, improving the average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%. Analyses further show that harness and policy improvements are complementary and that Self-HPO improves reliability (pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (pass@k) over the base agent.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: Agent implementation. We use Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the backbone and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) for model serving. RL and SFT use the slime framework on one node with eight B200 GPUs. The seed harness follows the mini-SWE-agent interface (Yang et al., 2024), through which the model executes bash commands in task-specific repository environment. Optimization data. The initial search set S0 consists of 300 tasks randomly sampled from the training data D. For subsequent H-steps, the search set consists of hard tasks from D, identified using the verified trajectories collected during the preceding P-step: task is hard if it is never resolved in any of its rollouts in that P-step. These task IDs are reused to generate fresh failure evidence with the updated policy at the next H-step. Harness optimization. Self-HPO uses the current policy checkpoint as both task solver and harness proposer. The proposer examines the experience of evaluated harnesses and their trajectories, including failed trajectories, and revises the current best harness. HPO instead uses Opus 4.8 to propose revisions, while retaining the same alternating H-stepP-step structure. In both configurations, each H-step evaluates = 6 candidates, each run once per search task, and the selected harness is held fixed during the next policy update. The Self-Harness and Meta-Harness baselines use the same search budget. Policy optimization. Each P-step initializes from the policy produced by the preceding round and collects on-policy trajectories under the updated harness. The executable verifier supplies outcome rewards, and the policy is optimized with GRPO and Balanced Adaptive Rollout (BAR) (Shao et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2026). Let A(τi) denote the assistant-generated token positions in trajectory τi, (cid:98)Ai its group-relative advantage, and ρi,u(θ) the ratio of updated-policy to rollout-policy token probabilities. The clipped objective is LP(θ) = i 1 A(τi) uA(τi) min (cid:16) ρi,u(θ) (cid:98)Ai, clip(ρi,u(θ), 1 εlow, 1 + εhigh) (cid:98)Ai , (2) (cid:17) where εlow = 0.2 and εhigh = 0.28 are the clipping thresholds. BAR generates eight rollouts per task and selects four to form reward-balanced group with success fraction between 0.25 and 0.75. Sampling continues until 32 groups pass filtering, yielding 128 training trajectories per batch. Each batch is optimized for one epoch with global batch size of 128, corresponding to one optimizer update. We use Adam with constant learning rate of 106, weight decay 0.01, an entropy coefficient of 104, and no KL penalty. Rollouts use temperature 0.95 and top-p 0.95. RLVR uses the same configuration under the seed harness, with 50 updates per P-step.

sections.title: C Conceptual Comparison with Related Methods
sections.content: Table 5 compares Self-HPO with Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026), Self-Harness (Zhang et al., 2026a), Task-CoEvolve (Miyai et al., 2026), Evo2 (Xu et al., 2026a), WHALE (Kim et al., 2026), and HASE (Luo et al., 2026) in terms of coverage of the coding domain, how the policy learns, who proposes harness changes, and how harness-search tasks are selected. The trained solver becomes the next harness proposer. Self-Harness revises its harness with fixed policy, WHALE uses frozen external proposer alongside policy learning, and Evo2 trains separate proposer while the task-solving policy stays frozen. Self-HPO instead reuses the updated task-solving policy as the proposer in the next round: the H-step holds policy weights fixed, and the P-step performs RL under the selected harness. HASE also trains self-proposing policy, but places task solving and harness editing in joint RL action space, with persistent edits reviewed at phase boundaries. Policy training also determines the next harness-search tasks. The P-step supplies two inputs to the next H-step: the updated proposer Pt+1 and search set St+1 drawn from hard tasks encountered during RL. Thus, policy learning changes both who proposes and which tasks guide the search. TaskCoEvolve also adapts task selection, but uses outcome variance across candidate harnesses within search rather than difficulty exposed during policy training. Self-HPO updates task IDs between H-steps and keeps them fixed within each H-step.

sections.content: Seed harness. The seed harness H0 is the mini-SWE-agent ReAct loop (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024): the agent issues bash tool calls in task-specific sandbox and ends the episode by printing the patch after fixed submission command. Its task prompt contains the issue description followed by fixed instructions, including the exact command used to submit the patch. Harness search space. candidate harness is Python class that subclasses the seed agent, together with its prompt templates. It may override the agents step, for example to inspect the agents state, return feedback before accepting submission, replace the submitted patch, or intervene at any step. All repository access goes through the sandbox. The policy and sampling configuration (temperature and top-p of 0.95) are fixed across candidates.
